questions.text: I find it satisfying to maintain cohesion as the group moves forward.
I notice when the physical distance between two people in a conversation is slightly greater than normal and read the reason for it.
I schedule appointments with buffer time between them to avoid feeling rushed.
I consistently set long-term goals and build step-by-step plans to reach them.
Other people's hardships tend to matter to me.
I tend to pick vacations based on what I want to see and do, not on what others prefer.
I redesign my approach each time I encounter a new problem rather than applying a formula.
I notice that when I feel passionate about something, it becomes all-consuming rather than a background interest.
When suffering is described in abstract terms, I still want something to improve for those affected.
I notice that surprises, interruptions, and disruptions produce only a small ripple in my internal state.
Small hardships in other people's lives rarely matter to me.
I bring concerns about a plan to the group rather than canceling it myself.
I sense when someone is being conspicuously silent to make their absence from the conversation felt.
I routinely evaluate friendships by whether they contribute to my personal development.
I am inclined to enforce standards even when the group has not explicitly agreed to them.
I would deplete my emergency fund to help a loved one avoid a crisis.
I feel a surge of energy when I declare a new direction for a team.
I take pride in my ability to think on my feet and handle the unexpected.
I notice that my body stays relaxed in situations that make other people tense.
I notice when someone adopts a casual posture to deliberately lower the perceived stakes of a conversation.
I prefer straightforward conversations where everything is on the table.
I prefer to own the relationship with external partners on behalf of the team.
I notice that I don't get swept up in the emotional energy of crowds or groups.
It is hard for me to stop thinking about someone who is suffering.
I tend not to register when a group's dynamic shifts because of a new piece of information.
I routinely keep a list of personal achievements and review it for motivation.
When several people need help, none of their situations weighs on me much.
When something touches me, the feeling doesn't just visit — it moves in and stays.
Hearing that someone has died or been badly hurt leaves me with little wish to reach out.
Five-year plans seem pointless to me because so much changes that they quickly become irrelevant.
I like when the scope of work is something the whole team defines together.
I experience the arrival of strong emotion as a wave that crests before I can brace for it.
I would postpone my own goals indefinitely if someone close to me needed my help.
I leave detailed notes for my future self when pausing a project mid-stream.
I rarely detect the difference between someone making small talk and someone trying to connect.
I instinctively offer my seat, my place in line, or my turn to someone else.
